title: The Power of Counterplay: Exploiting Weaknesses | Alapin Sicilian | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: We take Black and answer with the Sicilian, c5.
White develops the knight to f3 and we bring ours to c6.
White plays c3 — the Alapin. But this move order, with the knights already out, denies us the line I usually recommend.

Normally against the Alapin I like ...d5, and after the trade ...Nf6 — but with our knight already on c6, ...d5 would force a queen recapture. So here we choose between transposing with ...d5, a ...Nf6/...e5/...Nd5 setup, or the sharp sideline ...e5.
We take the risk with e5 — objectively White is a touch better with precise play, but it's hard to prove, and I want to test our improvisation in fresh territory.

White strikes with d4. Our ...e5 is risky mainly because it leaves a hole on d5 — but as in the Najdorf's ...e5 structures, that square can be well covered by our minor pieces, so it's far from the end of the world.
d4 is one of White's two main moves — the other is the Italian-style bishop to c4. It forces mass trades in the centre; ...d6 exists but lets White steer into an unpleasant endgame.
The centre pawns are swapped off.

White recaptures with the knight. This is essentially a Scotch, only with the c-pawns already gone — which slightly favours White, because our d6-square is tender: if we try the bishop to c5, as I like against a normal Scotch, White gets the extra shot of the knight to f5, exploiting d6.
So instead the knight to f6 — now White has no time for the knight to f5, because the e4-pawn hangs. We reach a Scotch-like game, a shade worse for us but very playable.

White develops the knight to c3 and we've transposed into a Four Knights Scotch. The main move is the bishop to b4, pressuring e4 — there's also the sharp ...Nxe4 — but let's keep it straightforward with the bishop to b4.
